prose.summary: A facilities manager keeps a building or a portfolio of buildings running: HVAC, security, cleaning contracts, the loading dock schedule, the fire panel that needs testing. People confuse this with property management, but property managers chase leases and tenant relationships while facilities managers keep the physical plant and the vendors who service it under control. The overlap with maintenance technician work is real (many postings ask for both), but the manager is the one who signs the contract and answers when the chiller fails at 2am.
prose.day_to_day: Mornings usually start with a walk-through, not a screen: checking that last night's cleaning crew showed, that the loading dock is clear, that nobody's propped a fire door open with a trash can. From there the week splits between solo desk work (budgets, vendor invoices, a maintenance log that needs updating) and time spent with people: a contractor walking you through a quote, a front-desk staffer flagging a complaint, a safety inspector who wants five minutes of your time that turns into forty. Preventive maintenance schedules get reviewed and adjusted constantly, since a missed filter change now is a compressor replacement in August. The part people look forward to is smaller than you'd think: the day a long-deferred repair finally gets funded and you watch it get fixed instead of patched again. Most weeks also include some customer-service moments, since half of this job is translating tenant or employee complaints into a work order a vendor can act on. It closes with the same walk-through it opened with, just later and darker.
prose.work_environment: This is an on-site job by nature: you cannot inspect a rooftop unit, check a stairwell, or watch a contractor's work from home, which is most of why the remote share sits at 2 percent. Expect a mix of office (for budgets and vendor calls) and physical building (for inspections, walk-throughs, and the occasional crawl into a mechanical room). Hours are steady most of the year but spike around seasonal changeovers (spring HVAC startup, winter storm prep) and whenever a lease renewal or audit forces a compliance deadline. Bad weeks come from equipment failing on a holiday weekend or a vendor no-show the day before an inspection, not from a heavy meeting calendar. The work is social in short, sharp bursts: quick, specific conversations rather than long collaborative stretches.
prose.getting_in: Most postings (42 percent) state an experience requirement, and the median asked for is 2 years, usually in maintenance, front-office operations, or a related facilities or property role. A four-year degree is required in a meaningful share of postings but waived in others, where employers accept a mix of trade coursework, a facilities certification, or several years of hands-on building operations experience instead. The slowest part is rarely the classroom; it's accumulating the breadth (HVAC basics, vendor negotiation, a bit of budgeting) that lets you run a building without calling a supervisor for every decision. People commonly stall right around that 2-year mark, stuck doing maintenance-technician-adjacent work without ever being handed procurement or budget authority. Getting a manager to hand you a vendor contract to negotiate, even a small one, is usually the fastest way past that wall.
prose.ladder: Early on you're responsible for keeping systems running: work orders closed, vendors showing up, inspections passed. The next step up adds budget ownership: you're now deciding which repairs get funded this quarter and which get deferred, and you're the one explaining that tradeoff to whoever controls the money. From there the ladder forks: some people move toward portfolio-level roles overseeing multiple sites (more budgeting, more procurement, less time on a specific rooftop), while others stay hands-on and go deep into a technical specialty like sustainability retrofits or life-safety systems. That fork tends to show up around the 5 to 8 year mark, once someone has run at least one full budget cycle solo.
prose.suits: People who come alive in this job like fixing things that stay fixed and like being the person a building depends on without anyone quite noticing until something breaks. A good day is a vendor showing up on time, a repair holding through a storm, or a tenant complaint resolved before it becomes an email chain to your boss. It suits someone who doesn't mind being interrupted constantly and can hold five half-finished tasks in their head without losing any of them. People who leave usually wanted deeper technical specialization (they go into HVAC or biomedical equipment specifically) or wanted out of the interruption cycle entirely, toward something with longer, quieter blocks of focused work.
prose.misconceptions: Outsiders assume this is a janitorial supervisor role, but the real center of the job is vendor management and budget decisions, not cleaning schedules. Another common assumption is that it's a desk job because 'manager' is in the title; in practice a large share of the week is spent walking the building, and the postings that mention front-office or customer-service skills (16 percent each) reflect how much of the job is direct, in-person problem solving rather than email.
prose.who_qualifies: Maintenance technicians carry over the most (a 32 percent match): they already know the equipment and the vocabulary, and mostly need to add budgeting and vendor negotiation. Warehouse managers and event planners also transfer well, since both jobs are built around coordinating multiple moving parts and vendors under a deadline, though they usually need to build up the equipment-specific knowledge (HVAC cycles, life-safety systems) that a maintenance background hands you for free. Biomedical engineers show up too, usually moving from equipment-specific facilities work in hospitals into general building operations.
prose.what_the_numbers_miss: The postings can't show you what it feels like to be the one person everyone calls when the building itself goes wrong, at any hour, regardless of what else is on your plate. They also don't capture how much of the job is judgment calls about which of ten broken things to fix first with a budget that only covers three.

steps.do: Get 1 to 2 years of building operations experience
steps.how: Work as a maintenance technician, front-office coordinator, or building operations assistant. This is where you learn the equipment and the vocabulary; most facilities manager postings expect around 2 years of this before considering you.

Ask to shadow or run the PM schedule for a rooftop unit, elevator, or fire system for at least one full seasonal cycle. You'll know you're ready when you can explain why a filter change matters more in March than in July.

steps.do: Take on one vendor contract or small budget
steps.how: Negotiate a single service contract (landscaping, pest control, cleaning) start to finish: get quotes, pick a vendor, manage the relationship for a year. This is the fastest way to prove budget judgment before you're handed a full facilities budget.

steps.do: Pursue a facilities-specific certification if no degree
steps.how: If you don't have a four-year degree, a facilities management certification (the kind employers list as accepted in place of one) signals you know procurement, sustainability basics, and compliance. Expect a few months of study alongside your current job.

steps.do: Apply once you can own a full budget cycle
steps.how: Target postings that mention procurement and budgeting explicitly, not just maintenance. You're ready when you can walk into an interview and describe one full year of decisions you made about what got fixed, deferred, or replaced.

prose.tools: The real gatekeepers are facilities operations platforms (work order systems, PM scheduling software) and basic procurement or budgeting tools, since those show up in roughly a third of postings. Customer-service and front-office skills matter almost as much as the technical side, since a good chunk of the job is fielding complaints before they escalate. Sustainability tracking tools are showing up more often now, as postings increasingly ask for experience managing energy use or waste contracts, not just fixing what breaks.

industries.name: Corporate real estate
industries.note: Managing office campuses for a single employer; steady hours, heavy focus on tenant experience and lease-driven deadlines.

industries.name: Healthcare facilities
industries.note: Hospitals and clinics, where compliance and life-safety systems dominate and downtime has immediate consequences for patients.

industries.name: Property management firms
industries.note: Managing multiple client buildings at once; more travel between sites, more vendor negotiation, less time embedded in one building's culture.

industries.name: Manufacturing and warehousing
industries.note: Keeping production-critical infrastructure running; less customer-facing, more focused on equipment uptime and safety compliance.

specializations.name: Sustainability and energy management
specializations.why: Shows up in 13 percent of postings and growing; employers with aggressive energy-reduction targets are paying for people who can run retrofit projects and track savings.

specializations.name: Life-safety and compliance systems
specializations.why: Hospitals and large commercial portfolios need someone who owns fire systems, code inspections, and audits; it's technical enough to insulate you from generalist competition.

specializations.name: Multi-site portfolio operations
specializations.why: Once you've run one building well, overseeing several is a natural next step and pays toward the higher end of the range, since it adds procurement scale and cross-site budget authority.

pros: You get to see the direct result of your decisions: a repair you funded holds through a storm, a vendor you picked shows up on time for a year straight.
The job stays varied because no two days have the same mix of problems, from a broken elevator to a lease compliance question.
It's one of the few management roles where you're still allowed, even expected, to get your hands on the actual equipment.
Demand is steady and spread across almost every industry, so the skills transfer if you want to change sectors without changing careers.
cons: You're the person who gets called when something breaks at an inconvenient hour, and that doesn't fully go away as you get more senior.
A lot of the job is triage: deciding which of several urgent problems gets the budget this quarter, which means something always waits.
The remote share is basically zero, so this isn't a career you can do from a different city than your building.
Vendor relationships take real time to build, and a bad one (a contractor who no-shows, a supplier who overcharges) can eat a week you didn't have to spare.

faq.q: how long does it take to become a facilities manager
faq.a: Most people spend around 2 years in a maintenance, front-office, or operations role before stepping into the title, based on the experience level most postings ask for. Getting real budget or vendor-negotiation experience during that time matters more than the calendar length.

faq.q: do you need a degree to be a facilities manager
faq.a: No, not always: a degree is required in a meaningful share of postings but waived in others, where a facilities certification plus hands-on experience is accepted instead. What employers want is proof you can run a maintenance schedule and manage a vendor contract, degree or not.

faq.q: facilities manager vs property manager, what's the difference
faq.a: A facilities manager owns the physical building and its systems (HVAC, maintenance, vendors), while a property manager owns the tenant and lease relationship. The two roles often work side by side in commercial real estate, but facilities management leans technical and property management leans commercial and legal.

Barely: the remote share sits at just 2 percent, since the core of the job is physically inspecting equipment and buildings. Some budgeting and vendor calls can be done remotely, but the walk-throughs and on-site problem-solving can't.

faq.q: what does a facilities manager get paid starting out
faq.a: Entry-level pay in this field runs toward the lower end of the measured range, with the middle of the market sitting well above that once you've got a few years and a budget under your belt. Pay tends to climb fastest once you move from managing one site to overseeing several.
